title: THE BIBLE WARNS AGAINST ADULTERY—Then Immediately Celebrates Sexual Delight in Marriage
paragraphs: THE BIBLE WARNS AGAINST ADULTERY—Then Immediately Celebrates Sexual Delight in Marriage
Proverbs 5 does something many Christians are almost afraid to do: it warns you about the bed that can destroy your life… then tells a husband to rejoice deeply in the wife God has given him.
Because the Bible does not merely say, “Do not commit adultery.”
It does something far more confronting.
It takes you to the edge of forbidden desire.
It shows you the sweetness.
It shows you the seduction.
It shows you the aftermath.
And then—almost without warning—it turns around and celebrates passionate delight inside marriage.
That matters.

Because perhaps one of the great tragedies in Christian conversations about sexuality is that we have sometimes spoken loudly about what God forbids while whispering about what God created to be good.
Proverbs 5 does neither.
It does not blush at marital desire.
And it does not romanticize adultery.
It tells the truth about both.
Listen carefully to the opening warning:
“For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.”
That is Proverbs 5:3–4 in the King James Version.
The Hebrew makes the contrast even more vivid.
The forbidden woman’s lips are described as dripping נֹפֶת — nōp̄eṯ, honey or sweetness.
Her speech is smoother than שֶׁמֶן — shemen, oil.
But her end is מָרָה — mārāh.
Bitter.
That is temptation in one devastating picture.
Sweet at the entrance.
Bitter at the end.
And somebody reading this already knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe your temptation did not begin in a bedroom.
Maybe it began with a message.
A notification.
A conversation you knew was becoming too personal.
A coworker who seemed to understand you in ways your spouse no longer seemed to.
An old relationship you searched for “just to see how they were doing.”
A private browser.
A second account.
A friendship you kept defending because technically, technically, technically…
“Nothing happened.”
But something was happening inside you.
Your heart had begun traveling somewhere your body had not yet gone.
And that is why Proverbs is so mercifully ruthless.
God does not merely warn us about the moment of adultery.
He warns us about the road leading there.
“Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house.”
Not merely her bed.
Her door.
There are doors you do not prove your strength by standing beside.
There are conversations you do not continue to demonstrate your maturity.
There are temptations you do not negotiate with.
There are messages you do not need to answer.
There are relationships you do not need to “manage.”
Sometimes wisdom looks remarkably unheroic.
You leave.
You block.
You confess.
You tell your spouse.
You call somebody mature enough to hold you accountable.
You stop pretending that secrecy is harmless simply because nobody has caught you yet.
Because sin almost always makes promises about the beginning while hiding the ending.
Proverbs shows you the ending.
Years lost.
Honor given away.
Strength consumed.
Regret arriving when consequences can no longer be undone.
Until the person finally cries:
“How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof…”
That may be one of the saddest moments in the chapter.
Not because the sinner lacked warnings.
Because the sinner had warnings and kept walking.
Imagine realizing that the voice you called restrictive was actually trying to rescue you.
Imagine discovering that the boundary you resented was a guardrail beside a cliff.
That is biblical sexual holiness.
God is not standing between you and joy.
He is standing between you and the counterfeit that promises joy while quietly sharpening a knife.
But then Proverbs 5 does something extraordinary.
After warning against illicit sexual desire, Scripture does not conclude:
“Therefore, desire itself is dirty.”
It turns toward marriage.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then comes the line:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
The Hebrew word translated “rejoice” is שָׂמַח — śāmaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
This is not reluctant tolerance.
This is not cold obligation.
This is delight under covenant.
And then Scripture becomes even more intimate:
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And no, Proverbs does not apologize for it.
The Hebrew behind “be thou ravished” is related to שָׁגָה — shāgāh, a word that can convey being captivated, enraptured, even overwhelmed.
Read the contrast carefully.
The chapter is not contrasting sexuality with holiness.
It is contrasting covenant delight with covenant-breaking desire.
That changes everything.
God is not anti-sex.
God created human beings male and female.
God created marriage.
God created the body.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture can speak of sexual delight without treating it as filthy.
The problem is not that desire exists.
The question is where desire is taking you.
Toward covenant?
Or away from it?
Toward faithfulness?
Or secrecy?
Toward giving yourself faithfully to your spouse?
Or consuming another person in your imagination?
Toward gratitude?
Or endless appetite?
Because Proverbs 5 asks a haunting question:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
In other words:
Why abandon the fountain God has given you to chase water that cannot satisfy?
And then comes the verse that destroys the illusion of secret sin:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
Before the eyes of the LORD.
The Hebrew name there is יְהוָה — YHWH, the covenant name of God.
The hidden messages.
Before Him.
The deleted history.
Before Him.
The fantasies nobody knows about.
Before Him.
The emotional affair you keep renaming “friendship.”
Before Him.
The loneliness inside your marriage.
Before Him.
The wounds that made forbidden attention feel intoxicating.
Before Him.
The temptation you have resisted for months and never told anybody about.
Before Him too.
And that last part matters.
Because God does not merely see the person falling.
He sees the person fighting.
He sees the husband turning his eyes away.
He sees the wife refusing emotional intimacy that belongs inside her covenant.
He sees the believer deleting what needs to be deleted.
He sees the trembling confession.
He sees the tears.
He sees the marriage trying to heal after betrayal.
He sees the spouse wondering whether trust can ever live again.
He sees the person ashamed of what they have become.
And perhaps that person is you.
So what happens if Proverbs 5 did not reach you before the fall?
What happens when the warning comes after the affair?
After the pornography?
After the messages?
After the secret relationship?
After the betrayal?
After you became the person you once swore you would never become?
This is where we must read Proverbs 5 inside the larger story of Scripture.
The Bible does not minimize sexual sin.
But neither does the Gospel declare sexual sinners beyond redemption.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully kept every stain off their history.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin—not imaginary sin, sanitized sin, socially acceptable sin, but real sin.
Ugly sin.
Secret sin.
Sexual sin.
Pride.
Deception.
Lust.
Adultery.
Hypocrisy.
The sins we confess publicly and the sins we would rather die than have projected onto a screen.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says it was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
And the resurrection says your sin does not get the final word.
Repentance is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not permission to return to the same chains.
Jesus forgives—and Jesus calls people out of darkness.
That is why grace is so much greater than religious image management.
You can protect an image while your soul is dying.
You can sing worship songs while hiding messages.
You can quote Scripture while feeding an addiction.
You can sit beside your spouse in church while emotionally belonging to somebody else.
You can convince everybody.
Except God.
And strangely, that may be the beginning of hope.
Because the God who already knows everything is still calling you into the light.
You do not have to manufacture innocence.
You need mercy.
You need repentance.
You need Christ.
If you have never crossed the physical line but you know your heart is getting dangerously close, do not wait for catastrophe to make you serious.
Move away from the door.
If your marriage has become cold, do not use its pain as permission to build another relationship in secret.
Seek help.
Speak truth.
Pray.
Listen.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Relearn tenderness.
Pursue your spouse.
Protect your covenant.
And where serious betrayal, abuse, coercion, or danger exists, seeking wise pastoral and qualified professional help is not faithlessness. Safety and truth matter.
If you have already fallen, stop building your future around hiding your past.
Bring sin into the light.
Confess to God.
Turn away from it.
Seek wise accountability.
Where you have harmed others, take responsibility without demanding instant trust or cheap forgiveness.
Repentance has fruit.
Restoration may take time.
Consequences do not always disappear.
But shame does not have to become your permanent identity.
Because there is a difference between being exposed by sin and being defined by sin.
Peter failed.
David fell terribly and suffered consequences.
The Corinthian church included people with deeply broken sexual histories, yet Paul could write:
Were.
Then:
“But ye are washed…”
“But ye are sanctified…”
“But ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Do not turn grace into an excuse to keep sinning.
But do not turn your past into a throne more powerful than the cross either.
Jesus Christ is greater.
Maybe you are reading this beside someone you love while knowing there is something on your phone they have never seen.
Maybe your spouse is asleep.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe you have not touched another person, but your imagination has been living somewhere else for months.
Maybe you are the betrayed one, and every sentence in this article hurts because you did not choose the scandal that entered your home.
Maybe you are single and wondering whether any of this applies to you.
It does.
Proverbs is teaching all of us what desire becomes when wisdom no longer governs it.
Sexual integrity begins long before marriage and matters long after the wedding photographs have faded.
And if you are married, hear what Proverbs 5 refuses to let religious shame erase:
Faithfulness is not merely refusing everybody else.
It is learning again to delight in the covenant God has entrusted to you.
See your spouse.
Talk.
Touch with tenderness.
Listen.
Flirt with your spouse instead of feeding attention somewhere else.
Protect time together.
Pray together.
Forgive.
Get help when you need it.
Remember that marriage is made of two imperfect people who need grace every morning.

And never confuse marital sexual delight with entitlement. Biblical intimacy is not coercion. Love does not use another person's body. Christian marriage calls husband and wife to faithful, self-giving love, honor, tenderness, and mutual care.
The world often tells us that freedom means removing boundaries.
Proverbs gives another picture.
Some boundaries protect the very thing you hope will remain beautiful.
A fireplace is warm because the fire has a place to burn.
Outside that place, the same fire can consume the house.
Desire needs covenant.
Passion needs faithfulness.
Pleasure needs wisdom.
And sinners need grace.
That is why Proverbs 5 is not merely a warning about adultery.
It is an invitation to stop drinking poison while calling it honey.
It is an invitation to come home.
And perhaps somebody needs to come home tonight.
Not merely to a spouse.
To God.
No more hiding.
No more rehearsing excuses.
No more waiting until consequences force the confession your conscience has been begging you to make.
Jesus already knows.
Come into the light.
One wife may need courage to speak.
One young person may need to understand that God's boundaries are not hatred of pleasure.
One secret sinner may finally confess.
One shattered spouse may discover that Christ has not abandoned them.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too. Sometimes sharing truth is one of the simplest ways we can place a light where someone in darkness might see it.
It does not.
Not because giving money can purchase forgiveness or blessing.
It cannot.

Rather, Scripture teaches willing, generous support for Gospel work. Paul wrote that giving should be purposeful and not coerced—“not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7)—and he also taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for that work (1 Corinthians 9:14).
So pray about it.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, creating, and putting Christ-centered resources into the hands of people who need them.
Send it privately to someone you love.
Pray for the ministry.
Keep pointing people toward Jesus.
The mission is Christ.
The sinner coming home.
The marriage being protected.
The hidden sin being confessed.
The wounded heart discovering grace.
The tempted believer choosing the narrow road.
The ashamed person discovering that the cross is not frightened by their history.
The lost hearing that Jesus still saves.
Proverbs 5 begins with a father pleading with his son to listen.
Thousands of years later, the warning still reaches us.
Honey can become bitter.
Secret roads can become chains.
A moment can become a wound that lasts for years.
But you do not have to keep walking toward the door.
Turn around.
And if you already walked through it…
turn around anyway.
There is still a Savior.
There is still repentance.
There is still grace.
There is still a cross where guilty people can kneel.
There is still an empty tomb declaring that death, shame, and sin do not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs to carry with them after everything else here fades:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when you surrender the pen to Jesus, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
